classification.difficultyReason: Polynomial factor induction needs an add-and-subtract rewrite in part a and an x^2 step of 2 in part b. This is harder than the x-1 case.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $x-2$ is a factor of $x^n-2^n$ for all integers $n\geq1$.

answer.short: The base case is $x-2$. If $x^k-2^k=(x-2)p(x)$, then $x^{k+1}-2^{k+1}=(x-2)(xp(x)+2^k)$, so the result follows by induction.
answer.worked:
Test $n=1$.
$$\mathrm{LHS}=x^1-2^1=x-2.$$
Therefore the statement is true for $n=1$.

Assume true for $n=k$, where $k\geq1$:
$$x^k-2^k=(x-2)p(x),$$
where $p(x)$ is a polynomial.

Prove $n=k+1$.
WTP: $x^{k+1}-2^{k+1}=(x-2)q(x)$, where $q(x)$ is a polynomial.
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=x^{k+1}-2^{k+1}\\&=x\times x^k-2\times2^k\\&=x[(x-2)p(x)+2^k]-2\times2^k\quad\text{using assumption}\\&=x(x-2)p(x)+2^k(x-2)\\&=(x-2)(xp(x)+2^k)\\&=(x-2)q(x)\end{align*}$$
Here $q(x)=xp(x)+2^k$ is a polynomial.

The statement is true for $n=1$, and truth for $n=k$ implies truth for $n=k+1$. By mathematical induction, it is true for all integers $n\geq1$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $x+1$ is a factor of $x^{2n}-1$ for all integers $n\geq1$.

answer.short: The base case is $(x+1)(x-1)$. If $x^{2k}-1=(x+1)p(x)$, then $x^{2k+2}-1=(x+1)(x^2p(x)+x-1)$, so the result follows by induction.
answer.worked:
Test $n=1$.
$$\mathrm{LHS}=x^2-1=(x+1)(x-1).$$
Therefore the statement is true for $n=1$.

Assume true for $n=k$, where $k\geq1$:
$$x^{2k}-1=(x+1)p(x),$$
where $p(x)$ is a polynomial.

Prove $n=k+1$.
WTP: $x^{2(k+1)}-1=(x+1)q(x)$, where $q(x)$ is a polynomial.
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{LHS}&=x^{2k+2}-1\\&=x^2\times x^{2k}-1\\&=x^2[(x+1)p(x)+1]-1\quad\text{using assumption}\\&=x^2(x+1)p(x)+x^2-1\\&=x^2(x+1)p(x)+(x+1)(x-1)\\&=(x+1)(x^2p(x)+x-1)\\&=(x+1)q(x)\end{align*}$$
Here $q(x)=x^2p(x)+x-1$ is a polynomial.

The statement is true for $n=1$, and truth for $n=k$ implies truth for $n=k+1$. By mathematical induction, it is true for all integers $n\geq1$.
